person.name: Andrew Still
person.headline: Design systems for all
person.intro: New York City based Design System Specialist with over 5 years of experience across design systems design, development and enablement.

deepDives.label: Agents
deepDives.title: Agents can use it without breaking it
deepDives.summary: People and agents go through the same checks.
body: A server shares the tokens, specs and docs over MCP. An agent working in another project can search the system, read a component’s spec, style with semantic tokens and check a new color pairing before using it.
Editing needs a key. When an agent changes a token, contrast is checked again. If a pair fails, the change is undone and the agent gets the failing pairs back so it can try another value.
This portfolio was built that way. The agent that wrote it pulled component specs and tokens from Lock In instead of guessing.

figure.alt: An agent reads a component spec, then updates a token. Three contrast pairs fail, the file is restored and the agent receives a 422 listing them.

deepDives.label: Spec
deepDives.title: One spec, checked against the code
deepDives.summary: The build fails if React, React Native and the spec disagree.
body: Each component has one JSON spec listing its props, states, tokens, accessibility rules and usage. Code, Figma, docs and agents all read from it.
On every pull request, a script compares the React and React Native props with the spec. A missing prop, a different default or a mismatched option fails the build.
Figma can’t mirror code exactly, so the spec also records how each prop maps to Figma, including the 52 places where the two differ on purpose.

figure.alt: A component spec feeds the Figma props map and the get_component tool. A check script compares it with the React and React Native prop types and fails the build on drift.

deepDives.label: Contrast
deepDives.title: Contrast is checked on every build
deepDives.summary: 486 checks across light, dark and two themes.
body: Components use semantic color tokens, like “text primary,” which point to the base palette in light and dark mode. Themes only change those semantic tokens, so raw colors never reach a component.
Each token build checks 81 text and background pairs in every mode and theme. Text needs a 4.5:1 ratio, and borders and focus rings need 3:1. If any pair misses, the build fails and lists it.
When a check fails, the fix is a different token. The requirement never gets lowered.

figure.alt: A token edit resolves aliases per mode and theme and runs the contrast pairs. If every pair passes, outputs are emitted; otherwise the build fails with the failing pairs.

deepDives.label: Figma
deepDives.title: Figma and code, mapped prop by prop
deepDives.summary: Figma Variables come from the tokens, and every component has Code Connect.
body: Code is the source of truth. A script turns the tokens into Figma Variables, with light and dark modes for each theme, and every variable shows the same CSS name engineers use.
Each spec maps its props to Figma: 214 rows across 15 components. Where the two differ, a note explains how. The loading prop in code, for example, is state=loading in Figma.
Code Connect covers 20 Figma components and 33 icons, so Dev Mode shows real Lock In code with the props the designer picked.

deepDives.label: Governance
deepDives.title: Gaps become proposals
deepDives.summary: New components come in as proposals with evidence, and the owner decides.
body: When a product needs something Lock In doesn’t have, it files a proposal instead of building a private workaround. The proposal explains the problem, shows where else it’s needed, says why no existing component fits and includes a draft spec. Agents file through MCP and people through a GitHub form.

I triage each one. Does more than one product need it? Could an existing component take a variant instead? Is the accessibility pattern settled? Once a proposal is accepted, a workflow opens a draft pull request with the spec, web and native code, stories and docs.
Retired components stay for at least one minor release, with a note pointing to the replacement.

The first proposal, Textarea, came from an agent working on VolleyXP. InputField couldn’t cover it, because a single-line input can’t wrap and Enter behaves differently. Textarea shipped on web and native with Code Connect, and VolleyXP replaced its workaround with it.

figure.alt: Lifecycle of a Lock In proposal: filed through the hub by an agent or through the GitHub issue form, it moves from proposed through triage, accepted and in code to released, with an optional in-design route and declined as the other outcome. Each status label runs the proposals workflow, which records it in the proposal file.

experience.title: Specs, handoff and visual QA
experience.summary: A contract on Verizon’s design system team, making sure system updates made it from Figma into code accurately.
points: Managed the handoff of design system updates from design to development.
Wrote specs in Figma for design system components and templates.
Led visual QA for new design system additions across Figma and Storybook.

experience.title: Teaching design systems from inside Figma
experience.summary: I ran internal enablement at Figma, teaching employees how Figma and design systems fit into product development and how to talk about them with customers.
points: Designed and led an internal training program on design systems, product design and software development.
Helped build a workflow sales teams used to measure the maturity of their customers’ design systems.
Rebuilt new-hire onboarding to cover how Figma works, where it fits in product development and how to talk about it with customers.

experience.title: Automated design tokens across CBS Sports
experience.summary: I worked on the design system behind CBS Sports’ brands and platforms, from the token pipeline to the React component library.
points: Set up an automated, end-to-end design token system across CBS Sports brands and platforms, which sped up development and kept teams aligned.
Worked with designers and developers to align component APIs between the Figma and React libraries.
Shipped functional and visual updates to the React component library.
Wrote documentation and educational content that made more people aware of the design system.

experience.title: Explaining technical products to the people who buy them
experience.summary: I was the technical resource for Imperva’s inside sales team. I worked with prospects on both the technical and business side to show how Imperva’s products could help them.
points: Stayed in touch with customers through the whole pre-sale process.
Analyzed usage statistics to find areas to improve, and taught customers how to use the product well.
